newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Analysts cool on Bank Austria plans.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Analysts cool on Bank Austria plans.

text.p: Bank Austria, sketching out its strategy after taking over rival Creditanstalt, on Monday announced a three billion schillings ($252 million) capital increase and plans to combine some investment banking and foreign operations.
Chief executive Gerhard Randa disappointed analysts, however, by insisting that Bank Austria and Creditanstalt would continue to exist side-by-side in the domestic market for at least five years.

"It is not a problem to have competition between two brand names with a common owner. It is an everyday occurence," he told a news conference. "I see the two brand-name strategy in place for the next five to 10 years."

Bank Austria won a six-year race to take on the Austrian government's 70 percent holding of Creditanstalt ordinary shares in January. Last week the European Commission gave the green light to the deal, which catapulted Bank Austria-Creditanstalt into Europe's top 30 banks.
Speaking for the first time about his strategy, Randa painted a bright picture of cooperation in investment banking, foreign activities and systems and product development.

"There is enormous potential for savings. The two banks are spending more than three billion schillings a year in systems development alone. Their parallel development in new markets is costing another three billion," he said.
He forecast synergy savings worth around five billion schillings in five years' time but conceded costs would outweigh the financial benefits at the start.
"We expect a burden of a few hundred million schillings in the first one to two years but little of that will be visible in our consolidated results," Randa said.
By bringing together the two banks' investment banking operations, the group would reap the benefits of their respective strengths.
Creditanstalt Investmentbank had a proven track record in Eastern Europe while Investmentbank Austria's expertise lay in privatisations, Randa said.

Analysts agreed that Bank Austria was taking a step in the right direction but said its policy of no compulsory redundancies at home and no aggressive downsizing of the domestic branch network would contribute little to the efficiency of Austrian banking.
"The 10-year time frame is too long. The density of banks in Austria is too great," said Alfred Reisenberger, Austrian analyst at IMI Sigeco in London.
"This isn't really much of a strategy. If Bank Austria had not bought Creditanstalt the picture would have been no different," said a second analyst who declined to be named.

Analysts were also cool to Randa's suggestion that the state should sell its 18.9 percent of Bank Austria ordinary stock, or 10.8 million shares, to coincide with the June issue of preference shares worth three billion schillings.
The preference share issue would work out at around 7.4 million shares based on Monday's close of 406 schillings.
"A capital increase was expected but maybe not that soon. It remains to be seen whether the market can absorb these shares," IMI Sigeco's Reisenberger said.
Gerhard Auer at ICE Securities in London said it was not easy to make a nice story out of Bank Austria because of a huge hangover of stock in public ownership.

Bank Austria is firmly in state hands and is among the most illiquid stocks in the Vienna bourse's ATX index. In addition to the state's 18.9 percent stake, the City of Vienna controls 45 percent of voting shares through its AVZ holding. ($ = 11.92 Austrian Schillings)
